description_full: BXP, Inc. is the largest publicly traded developer, owner, and manager of premier workplaces in the United States. It is concentrated in six dynamic gateway markets - Boston, Los Angeles, New York, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC. BXP has delivered places that power progress for our clients and communities for more than 55 years. BXP is a fully integrated real estate company, organized as a real estate investment trust (REIT). As of June 30, 2026, including properties owned by joint ventures, BXP's portfolio totals 51.1 million square feet and 164 properties, including six properties under construction/redevelopment. BXP's portfolio consists of 143 office properties, 13 retail properties, seven residential properties (including four residential properties under construction) and one hotel. BXP is well known for its in-house building management expertise and responsiveness to clients' needs. BXP holds a superior track record of developing premium Central Business District (CBD) office buildings, successful mixed-use complexes, suburban office centers and build-to-suit projects for a diverse array of creditworthy clients. BXP actively works to promote its growth and operations in a sustainable and responsible manner. BXP, Inc. was incorporated in 1970 in Delaware and is based in Massachusetts, Boston.

CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: BXP, Inc. is a large-cap real estate business with a $11.5B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +2.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $561M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.50× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 11% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.99, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.49 vs 5y 0.98), so read it loosely.
About $83.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 69% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $98.61, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 49%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $81.07 to $122 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 4.9% (above the risk-free rate).
The 20 covering analysts target $73.60 on average, 13% above the price.
The price implies 5.6% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 61% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.50x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 16%.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (5.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.42 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.9% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 3.4% over 10 years.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 1.5% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (19.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $2.2M sold).
It returns 5.6% a year to shareholders (4.3% in dividends).
It pays out 151% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 10.4% of the float, 8.3 days to cover.
people: With about 826 employees, each generates about $4.2M of revenue, 1.8x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 5.3% a year.
That works out to $680K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.7M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
